newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman to open its doors to foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Oman to open its doors to foreign investors.

text.p: Oman, the Gulf's most liberal economy, is throwing open its doors to foreign investors with a new law, expected to be passed soon, allowing them up to 49 percent ownership in all listed firms.

Brokers and financial analysts said on Wednesday the sultanate, which in October took a step to lure overseas cash by streamlining taxes on foreign and local firms, would issue the amendment to its foreign investment law within weeks.

"A second royal decree is awaiting signature. It is due literally any day or week and will automatically open up all publicly quoted companies to 49 percent foreign ownership," said David Andrews of brokers Gulf Investment Services.
"We think it will be passed very soon. It will force all firms to allow investment from foreigners up to 49 percent," said Financial Services general manager Waleed Nasser.

In 1995 Oman raised the foreign participation ceiling from 49 to 65 percent in special cases and 100 percent in exceptional circumstances. But this prompted few inflows because most companies' articles do not allow foreign ownership, and the then tax regime discriminated against firms with foreign shareholders.

"We could not ask companies before to amend their articles of association, because of the taxation law. Now that it has been amended we have asked all companies to include in their general assembly agendas to open up to foreigners," said Muscat Securities Market executive vice-president Ashraf al-Nabhany.
But the new investment law will mean "companies won't have to wait for shareholders' meetings to approve the amendment of articles of association," Nasser said by telephone from Muscat.
Sitting at the eastern edge of the Arabian peninsula, the small independent oil producer is trying to diversify its economy away from reliance on the 850,000-900,000 barrels it pumps daily.
A top priority is to attract foreign investment and unlike many big oil producers in the region, Oman already allows foreign firms a stake in its oil fields.

But outside the oil sector overseas capital is scarce. Foreigners, other than nationals of the five other Gulf states, have invested in only 13 of the 97 listed stocks. Most of the rest of the foreign cash goes to three Omani mutual funds.
Only about 10 percent of the eight-year-old market's total capitalisation of 1.62 billion ($4.3 billion) is foreign money.
Brokers are looking forward to increased foreign business and say some big funds have already started investing in Oman.
"It is going to make a big difference. Already, some serious foreign investors are looking around. Big banks and fund managers see Oman as a small emerging market," said Andrews.
British Bank of the Middle East, part of HSBC Holdings Plc, recently introduced custodian services in Oman ahead of the more liberal laws, senior manager Steve Page said.
"There has already been a substantial increase in the number of transactions we handle for (foreign) clients," Page added.
Despite the changes, analysts said there were still hurdles.
"The real obstacle is that the market is still very small. Volumes are growing but are tiny in global terms," said Andrews.
The average daily value of trade so far this year has been around two million rials, about double the 1996 average.
Nasser voiced concern that local firms' capital was too small and the market, which has shot up over six percent this year and 35 percent since early 1996, was overvalued.
"I'm afraid of increases in price. The yield is going down. The index is too high. There should be a correction, but still, demand is good," he said. ($1=0.38 rial)
